Thursday, 9 October. Elena calls Ioana. She has good news and worries. Julien is listening on speaker.
Ioana, I sent your birth certificate this morning. I’m glad it will arrive before the end of the month.
Thanks, Mum! And what about the trip in May? Have you looked at flights?
Yes. Your father and Radu will come with me. But there’s a problem: your grandmother.
What’s wrong with her? Is she ill?
No, no. But she has never flown. She’s eighty-one, and she’s very scared. I’m afraid she won’t want to come.
Oh no… It would be a real pity if she weren’t there. She’s the one who kept our secret!
I know. And there’s something else. She’s sorry you’re not getting married in church. For her, without a church, it isn’t really a wedding.
But Mum, in France the official wedding is at the town hall. And Julien is Catholic, I’m Orthodox…
Wait, Ioana. I have an idea. What if we had two ceremonies? The town hall in Lyon on 3 May, and the church in the village in the summer?
Julien… You would do that? So that she’d be happy?
Of course. I’m surprised nobody thought of it before! That way, your family wouldn’t need to fly twice.
And Granny could stay in Iași in May, if she’s too scared. We’d do a live video for her.
I’ll explain it to her this evening so that she understands. But I’m warning you: she’ll want the priest to be the village priest, and the whole family to come.
The whole family? How many people is that?
Oh… about a hundred and fifty. Although it’s a small village, we have a lot of cousins.
A hundred and fifty? (silence) Right. I’ll have to learn a lot more Romanian before summer comes.

“Kel vuh-y”: the subjunctive of vouloir. “Euille” = “uh-y”, as in “feuille” (leaf).
“Kuh voo voo ma-ree-yay”: two i’s in a row! The first is from the stem (mari-), the second from the ending -iez.
“Do-mazh”: stress on the last syllable. “Quel dommage !” = “kel do-mazh”: what a pity!
“Or-to-dox”: th is read as t, x = ks.
“Byẽ kuh”: nasal ien, as in “bien”. Always followed by the subjunctive.

When you express a feeling (joy, fear, regret, surprise) about what SOMEONE ELSE does, French uses the subjunctive. English says “I’m glad THAT you’re coming” (indicative), French says “je suis content que tu VIENNES” (subjunctive).
Je suis contente que vous veniez.
J’ai peur qu’elle ne veuille pas venir.
je regrette que / c’est dommage que
C’est dommage qu’elle ne soit pas là.
Je suis surpris que personne n’y ait pensé.
Je suis triste que tu partes.
Same subject → DE + infinitive: “Je suis content de venir.” (I’m glad, I’m coming). “J’ai peur de prendre l’avion.” (I’m afraid of flying.)
Some conjunctions are always followed by the subjunctive. Here are the most important:
Je t’explique pour que tu comprennes.
Bien que ce soit un petit village…
Je viens, à condition que tu sois là.
Il est parti sans que je le voie.
Careful: “après que” (after) takes the INDICATIVE, not the subjunctive, although many French people get it wrong. And “parce que” (because) also takes the indicative.
Same subject → preposition + infinitive: “pour comprendre”, “avant de partir”, “sans dire au revoir”.
The general rule: certain facts → indicative; wishes, feelings, necessities, doubts → subjunctive.
I want him to be there.
In careful French, after “avoir peur que” and “avant que” there is sometimes a “ne” that is NOT a negation. It’s called the “ne explétif”:
Let’s leave before it’s too late.
Don’t panic: it’s optional and sounds elegant. Romanian does something similar: “mi-e teamă să NU plouă” also means you’re afraid it will rain!
In France, a religious wedding can only take place AFTER the civil one. That’s why many mixed couples, like Ioana and Julien, have two ceremonies, sometimes in two countries.
I’m afraid he won’t be able to come.
Let’s go home before it gets dark.

All through October, in Iași, Radu tried to persuade his grandmother to fly. He showed her videos of planes on his phone. He explained to her that it was the safest means of transport in the world.
The grandmother listened politely, then always gave the same answer: “Although you’re right, my boy, I won’t get into that metal box. God gave us feet, not wings.”
Elena was starting to feel sad. She was afraid her mother would never see her granddaughter’s wedding except on a screen. And she knew her mother would be sad too, even if she didn’t say so.
One Sunday morning in November, the grandmother came into the kitchen with a newspaper in her hand. She put it on the table in front of Elena and pointed at a small ad with her finger.
“Iași – Lyon. Direct coach. Departs Thursdays. Thirty hours.” Elena looked at her mother. “Mum… You don’t mean that…”
“I do,” answered the grandmother. “I’m not afraid of coaches. I’ve taken coaches all my life. Radu just has to come with me, to carry my suitcase. And so that I don’t get bored.”

Radu, who was still asleep, was woken by his mother’s cries. When they explained, he sat up in bed, his hair all over the place. “Thirty hours on a coach? With Granny? She’ll make me eat sarmale for the whole journey!”
“That’s exactly what I’m going to do,” said the grandmother with a smile. “That way, you’ll understand what Julien went through.”
That same evening, Elena called Lyon. Ioana cried on the phone. Julien, for his part, laughed until he cried. “She’s going to cross the whole of Europe by coach for our wedding? At eighty-one?”
“She says she absolutely wants you to see her dance,” answered Elena. “She says it’s a pity people don’t dance enough in Lyon. She intends to put that right.”

The news went round the family in a single evening. In Annecy, Brigitte called straight away: “I’m glad she’s coming, but I’m afraid she’ll be too tired. She must come and rest at our place after the wedding.” Behind her, Pierre shouted: “And taste my bread!”
Madame Bernard, for her part, offered her guest room. “I want her to stay with me, two steps from your place. Victor will be delighted to have one more person to stroke him.”

A few days later, Radu sent his sister a message: “Good news: Granny has agreed to let me take my computer on the coach. Bad news: she’s already started preparing the sarmale for the journey. In November!”
The following Wednesday, Julien told Hélène the story. The old lady put down her cup of tea and laughed, a young laugh, almost the laugh of the girl from Lucette’s café.
“An eighty-one-year-old woman crossing Europe by coach to dance at a wedding… I’m glad she’s coming. We’re going to get on very well, she and I.”
“But you don’t speak the same language,” said Julien.
Hélène shrugged. “My boy, at our age you don’t need to speak the same language any more. It’s enough to have the same memories. A war, a love, a waltz… And a lot of patience with young people.”
On his way home, Julien opened his computer. He searched for “Romanian course for beginners”. There were six months left before 3 May. And now he had two grandmothers to impress.
That evening, Ioana wrote in her notebook, under the date 3 May: “Although it’s completely crazy, it’s Granny’s best idea ever. I must buy her a cushion for the coach.”
